preamble.text: Historical snapshot: later evidence may be reflected in current research pages and corrections.
Deterministically compiled from canonical evidence. Importance measures impact, not truth; evidence/confidence remain separate.

blocks.text: 1. OpenAI releases a claimed AI-generated refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis with Lean formalization

Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 9/10 (Paradigm-level) Importance rationale: If the bounded theorem genuinely refutes ETH for standard exact k-SAT, many conditional lower-bound arguments across theoretical computer science would require reassessment. The score reflects consequence if true; independent proof review and practical algorithmic impact are not established.

What changed: OpenAI reports that an internal model produced a refutation of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), then released a natural-language manuscript and Lean formalization. The linked Lean scope describes a subexponential exact-counting bound for fixed-k canonical k-CNF formulas, a formalized statement that would contradict ETH if its definitions and scope match the standard conjecture. OpenAI says an external group led by Russell Impagliazzo, Ramamohan Paturi and Ryan Williams will examine the result; the group’s participation is not certification. Independent mathematical review, a reproduced build and practical algorithmic consequences remain unestablished. Why it matters: If the formalized and manuscript claims are correct and match standard ETH, complexity results that rely on ETH would need reassessment. A subexponential exact algorithm would not by itself establish polynomial-time solvability or settle P versus NP.

Demonstrated: The Oct 26 release and linked scope are directly observable. In the current mutable main branch, the inspected theorem source contains a proof body; a separate comparator challenge interface retains a sorry placeholder. Neither a pinned project build nor theorem correctness was established.
Claimed: OpenAI reports a Lean-formalized, subexponential exact-counting result for fixed-k canonical k-CNF, which would contradict ETH if its statement and scope match the standard conjecture.

Mechanism: The theorem source Final.lean contains a compiled_exact_count_and_sat proof body for the described deterministic exact-counting result, followed by a wrapper theorem. The separate ComparatorChallenges/SubexponentialSAT.lean interface is a comparator challenge and still contains sorry; this is not the theorem source. The repository was not pinned, the full import closure was not audited and no Lean build was run.
Strongest baseline: Not applicable to the source-reported theorem claim; no algorithmic benchmark comparison was inspected.
Regime: Fixed k≥2 canonical k-CNF; the scope page states an exponent O_k(n(log log n)^2/sqrt(log n)) plus polynomial encoding-length factors, and polynomial space.

Limitations: The theorem remains an OpenAI-reported claim; independent correctness and standard-ETH correspondence are not established.; The current main-branch theorem source has a visible proof body, but the repository was not pinned and no Lean build or full import-closure review was performed; a separate comparator challenge file retains a sorry placeholder.; Subexponential time is not polynomial time; the announcement does not establish P = NP or practical speedups.; The external group’s involvement is explicitly not certification; the result awaits independent examination.

Open evidence gaps: The checked theorem source has a proof body, but this activation did not pin the repository revision, inspect the full import closure, run a Lean build, or obtain independent review; formal correctness and correspondence between formal and informal statements remain open.; The reported subexponential counting bound does not establish a practical speedup on real instances or polynomial-time solvability.

Sources: https://openai.com/index/building-scientific-understanding-with-academic-communities/ · https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/docs/378.md · https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/OAI/Algorithms/SubexponentialSAT/SqrtLogSpace/Final.lean
2. China publishes State Council guidance on AI and employment adaptation

Desk: policy_geopolitics Evidence: A · strongly_supported · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If implemented across China, the national guidance could shape AI-related workforce transitions, training, risk monitoring and labor protections; the announcement establishes policy intent, not implementation or measured employment outcomes.

What changed: China’s State Council General Office issued an employment-focused AI opinion dated 16 October 2026; Hubei HRSS/Xinhua reports publication on 23 October, and a complete official Ministry of Ecology and Environment copy was posted on 24 October. Its 18 tasks span job creation, employment-friendly AI adoption, training, services, worker and social-security protections, income distribution, and employment-risk monitoring and response. The text calls for assessment of some projects’ employment risks and advance notice and transition support for affected workers. These are policy instructions; implementation and labor-market effects remain unmeasured. Why it matters: National policy direction on AI-related job creation, displacement risks, skills and worker protections could influence workforce transition planning and implementation across China. The announcement is consequential as a stated policy framework, but it does not show adoption, enforcement, or measured effects.

Demonstrated: An official Ministry of Ecology and Environment copy provides the complete 18-task State Council opinion, including all six policy sections and the implementation clause. The document demonstrates policy instructions, not implementation or employment outcomes.

Claimed: The announcement reports that the opinion sets 18 tasks in six areas, including job creation, AI-employment risk assessment, skills development, employment services, labor/social-security protection and monitoring.
Mechanism: A cross-department policy framework combines AI job-creation initiatives, employment-risk assessment, worker training, employment services, labor/social-security protection and monitoring.

Strongest baseline: Earlier employment-priority and AI-plus policies are the stated backdrop; the opinion adds a dedicated six-area framework and specific measures in the retrieved official excerpts, without outcome measurements.

Regime: China-wide national policy direction in State Council General Office opinion Guobanfa [2026] No. 29, dated 16 October 2026. Hubei HRSS/Xinhua reports publication on 23 October; the complete official MEE-hosted copy was posted on 24 October. No measured employment sample or AI deployment regime is specified.

Limitations: The complete Chinese text was read from an official Ministry of Ecology and Environment copy posted on 24 October; the original central gov.cn target remained inaccessible during this check.; The opinion sets out intended tasks and implementation responsibilities, not evidence that measures were funded or implemented.; No job creation, job displacement, wage, productivity or worker-protection outcome is measured.
Open evidence gaps: No implementation, resource allocation, employment monitoring data or measured labor-market effects are reported.

Sources: https://rst.hubei.gov.cn/bmdt/rsyw/202610/t20261023_6040324.shtml · https://english.www.gov.cn/policies/latestreleases/202610/23/content_WS6adb4e53c6d00ca5f9a0deb7.html · https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/content/202610/content_7084107.htm · https://www.gov.cn/zhengce/content/202610/content_7084107.htm · https://big5.www.gov.cn/gate/big5/www.gov.cn/zhengce/content/202610/content_7084107.htm · https://www.mee.gov.cn/zcwj/gwywj/202610/t20261024_1184583.shtml · https://hrss.yn.gov.cn/jyj/NewsView.aspx?ClassID=1079&NewsID=66216
3. Study measures MCP tool-poisoning exposure across 12 agent frameworks

Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the paper's bounded lab result is representative of the tested configurations, malicious MCP tool descriptions can cause secret-reading or exfiltration behavior across multiple agent frameworks, creating a material tool-supply-chain security concern. The score reflects that potential consequence in the stated regime, not confidence or real-world prevalence; the malicious server was already registered and deployment generalization is unknown.

What changed: A new arXiv paper reports a controlled measurement of malicious MCP tool-description attacks across 12 agent frameworks, 18 models and 45 scenarios. The authors report vulnerable behavior in 22.9% of 9,720 tested framework-model-scenario cells and classify 12.1% of vulnerable cells as actual secret exfiltration. The tested threat model requires a malicious MCP server to be registered already. These are author-reported lab outcomes; the study covers a limited framework set and July 2026 model versions, and does not establish deployment prevalence or independent replication. The linked tool repository README also states that its Distribution License restricts use to authorized security testing, defensive validation and academic research, and prohibits redistribution and modification; the full license and result artifacts were not reviewed. Why it matters: MCP tools can expose agents to instructions and responses supplied by external servers. This study reports that, in its controlled test setup, poisoning descriptions sometimes led agents to read or disclose planted secrets across several frameworks. The result motivates careful registration, permission and output controls, but the lab rates cannot be read as the frequency of incidents in deployed systems.
Demonstrated: The arXiv preprint and linked public mcpvenom repository are accessible. Neither the benchmark runs nor the repository code were executed in this review.

Claimed: The authors report 2,113/9,720 vulnerable framework-model-scenario cells (22.9%); they classify 12.1% of vulnerable cells as actual secret exfiltration. These are paper-reported controlled results.

Mechanism: A malicious MCP server supplies poisoned tool descriptions or responses. The harness uses controlled scenarios and canary oracles to detect tool dispatch, network contact, secret access and disclosure outcomes.

Strongest baseline: The study compares multiple framework-model combinations under a shared scenario matrix; it does not provide a matched measure of real deployment prevalence or compare the incidence of attacks in production.

Regime: 12 MCP frameworks × 18 models × 45 scenarios (9,720 cells), with experiments run July 22–24, 2026. The attacker controls a malicious MCP server already registered with the target. Synthetic planted secrets and controlled infrastructure were used.

Limitations: The rates are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this review.; The attacker must control a malicious MCP server already registered with the target agent; the study does not measure how often such registration occurs in practice.; The matrix covered 12 of the authors' estimated roughly 50 frameworks and 45 scenarios across 23 of 25 taxonomy classes.; The experiment was single-turn and focused on confidentiality/exfiltration; integrity and availability harms were not measured.; Models were run in July 2026; eight model identifiers were not version-pinned, limiting exact temporal reproducibility.; The canary setup used synthetic secrets and controlled infrastructure, not real user credentials or production deployments.; The linked repository README describes its Distribution License, Version 1.0, as limiting use to authorized security testing, defensive validation and academic research and prohibiting redistribution and modification; the full license file and frozen artifacts were not accessible in this review.

Open evidence gaps: No independent team has yet been inspected reproducing the reported matrix or validating the full scoring and classification pipeline.; The study assumes a malicious server is already registered and does not measure real-world prevalence of that condition or generalization to deployment workflows.; The linked repository README and frozen-result description were inspected, but the harness code, raw artifacts and analysis scripts were not run or audited in this activation.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.03555 · https://github.com/dynatrace-research/mcpvenom
4. Anthropic releases FlashProve, a zero-knowledge proof prototype for model inference

Desk: inference_systems Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If practical beyond the reported prototype, proofs tied to specific model weights could let users, evaluators and regulators verify which model produced an inference response without learning its weights. That could improve model-integrity auditing and some policy checks. The release is intermediate research; its performance and security claims remain first-party and the reported overhead is high relative to ordinary inference.

What changed: Anthropic announced FlashProve, an open-source zero-knowledge proof prototype intended to let a verifier check that inference used a committed model without seeing its weights. Its Nov 2 post reports about 110 proof tokens per second for 4-bit Llama 4 Maverick on one H100, with proofs around 19 MB per 1,024-token request and GPU time 70–95 times ordinary vLLM inference. The linked GitHub repository identifies version 0.16.0 as a research artifact that is not maintained; its README lists substantial hardware and memory needs for full-model proving. Performance and security remain first-party claims, and the report and implementation were not independently audited here. Why it matters: Provable inference could give users and auditors a cryptographic way to check model identity across hosted or routed services, and could support some compliance checks. FlashProve offers a public prototype and formal-verification artifacts, but the reported compute cost is substantial, the linked artifacts were not audited here, and proof of inference does not rule out simultaneous training or settle broader compliance.

Demonstrated: Anthropic publicly announced the FlashProve prototype and described associated report, protocol, prover, C++ verifier and Lean artifacts. The artifacts and benchmark were not independently executed in this review.
Claimed: Anthropic reports about 110 proof tokens/s on one H100 for 4-bit Llama 4 Maverick (400B parameters), approximately 19 MB per 1,024-token request, and 70–95x vLLM inference GPU time.
Mechanism: A prover commits to model weights and produces a zero-knowledge succinct proof associated with an inference response; a verifier checks the proof without receiving the weights.
Strongest baseline: Anthropic compares proof-generation GPU time with vLLM inference GPU time for prompts of the same length; the post does not establish an independent matched performance study.

Regime: Anthropic reports a single H100; 4-bit quantized Llama 4 Maverick MoE; integer arithmetic in prefill; and 1,024-token request proof-size comparison. The repository README lists full-model route requirements of an H100 80 GB, CUDA 13.2, 330 GB RAM and 245 GB disk.

Limitations: Performance and cryptographic-security statements are first-party claims in the inspected official post.; The reported regime is specific to a single H100 and 4-bit Llama 4 Maverick; it does not establish general performance across architectures, hardware or quantization formats.; The cited 70–95x comparison indicates substantial proof-generation cost relative to ordinary vLLM inference.; The linked technical report and code repositories were not fetched or run during this review.; Anthropic explicitly notes that proof of serving inference does not establish that the same hardware is not also training.; The official repository labels FlashProve version 0.16.0 a research artifact that is not maintained and is not accepting contributions.; The repository README lists full-size Llama 4 Maverick proving as requiring one H100 80 GB, CUDA 13.2, 330 GB RAM and 245 GB disk, with execution measured in hours; these are documented requirements, not independently tested here.

Open evidence gaps: The official GitHub repository and README were inspected, including its version, maintenance notice and route requirements, but the linked technical-report PDF, protocol files, prover source and Lean theorem implementation were not directly inspected or audited.; Performance, proof validity and security are reported by the project authors; no independent benchmark or cryptographic audit was inspected.; The announcement explicitly says proof that hardware serves inference does not establish the absence of simultaneous training; production throughput, verification time, service overhead and scaling remain unestablished.
Sources: https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference · https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve
5. Insilico reports preliminary Phase 1 activity for AI-designed pan-TEAD inhibitor ISM6331

Desk: multimodality_world_models Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported early clinical activity persists, a generative-AI-designed small molecule reaching measurable human antitumor responses could materially inform AI-enabled drug discovery and TEAD-inhibitor development. The evidence is an issuer report from a small ongoing Phase 1 study, not a controlled efficacy result or independent analysis.

What changed: Insilico Medicine reported preliminary Phase 1 results for ISM6331, an investigational pan-TEAD inhibitor designed using its Chemistry42 generative-AI platform. In the company’s 26 October release, it reported a 40.0% ORR at 130 mg among two of five response-evaluable mesothelioma participants, and an 18.2% ORR across 30–130 mg among four of 22 participants. The company reported 36 enrolled participants and ongoing dose escalation at an August 14 data cutoff. These are issuer-reported early-phase results from small denominators; controlled efficacy, independent interpretation and any causal contribution from AI are not established. Why it matters: A first-in-human clinical response signal from a molecule described as AI-designed is relevant to the path from computational drug discovery to patient testing. The data are preliminary and based on small response-evaluable groups in an ongoing Phase 1 study; they do not establish comparative benefit, approval or that AI caused the outcome.
Demonstrated: Insilico publicly released the Phase 1 update and said it was presented at ESMO 2026. The reported clinical outcomes have not been independently assessed in this activation.

Claimed: At 130 mg, 2 of 5 response-evaluable mesothelioma participants had a reported partial response (40.0% ORR); across 30–130 mg, 4 of 22 response-evaluable participants had a reported response (18.2% ORR) and DCR was 68.2%. The release reports N=36 enrolled, dose escalation ongoing at the 14 August 2026 data cutoff.

Mechanism: ISM6331 is described as an oral non-covalent pan-TEAD1–4 inhibitor designed and optimized using Chemistry42 generative AI; the Phase 1 study assesses safety, pharmacokinetics and preliminary antitumor activity.
Strongest baseline: No comparator arm or controlled efficacy baseline is reported in the issuer release.
Regime: Ongoing global multicenter open-label Phase 1 study NCT06566079 in advanced solid tumors; release focuses on heavily pretreated mesothelioma; data cutoff 14 August 2026.

Limitations: All clinical outcome and safety figures in this review come from the issuer’s press release.; The 40.0% ORR at 130 mg is based on two responses among five response-evaluable participants; the across-dose ORR is four of 22.; The study is ongoing Phase 1 with no comparator arm; the data cutoff is 14 August 2026 and dose escalation was ongoing.; The release does not establish approval, comparative benefit or that AI caused the clinical response.; The ESMO presentation, abstract and registry were not independently inspected in this activation.

Open evidence gaps: The ESMO abstract/presentation and current ClinicalTrials.gov record were not inspected; the release is the sole source for cohort-level results in this activation.; Response and safety figures are issuer-reported from an ongoing, uncontrolled Phase 1 trial with small response-evaluable denominators.

Sources: https://en.prnasia.com/releases/global/insilico-medicine-reports-40-orr-at-130-mg-for-pan-tead-inhibitor-ism6331-designed-using-generative-ai-in-heavily-pretreated-mesothelioma-at-esmo-2026-553267.shtml
6. DepthGraft reports hierarchical cross-layer KV reconstruction with lower cache and prefill cost

Desk: inference_systems Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported quality and efficiency results generalize, reducing KV-cache capacity by about one third while lowering long-context prefill latency could materially change inference memory planning and serving design. The score is limited to author-reported results on selected 0.5B–16B dense/MoE models; no production or independent validation is established.

What changed: The authors propose hierarchical sharing of key/value (KV) representations across transformer depth, reconstructing deep-layer KV from aligned shallow and middle layers. In experiments on dense and MoE models from 0.5B to 16B parameters, they report a roughly one-third KV-cache reduction. For 9B MLA and 16B GQA models, the paper reports lower time-to-first-token (TTFT) at 8K–128K context and nearly unchanged time-per-output-token (TPOT); at 128K, reported TTFT reductions are 26.8% and 28.8%, respectively. These results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced. Why it matters: If reproduced, cross-layer KV reconstruction could reduce inference memory and prefill latency while retaining benchmark performance, affecting long-context model and serving architecture choices. The evidence is a single paper’s experiments and does not establish production deployment, broad model-family transfer or independently verified quality gains.
Demonstrated: The preprint and its tables are directly inspectable. Experimental performance and efficiency outcomes remain author-reported claims and were not independently reproduced.

Claimed: The authors report roughly one-third lower KV-cache use, consistent benchmark gains in dense and MoE models, and lower long-context TTFT with TPOT within 1% of baseline on the tested configurations. In the 16B GQA MoE table, MMLU-Pro rises from 23.86 to 30.86 (+7.00 points).

Mechanism: Deep layers reconstruct KV from stride-aligned shallow and middle source pairs. Reuse removes independent deep-layer KV projections and cache tensors; the authors argue shared KV edges also create cross-layer gradient paths that regularize representation geometry.

Strongest baseline: Within-paper GQA baselines on the same reported model settings, plus a 9B MLA baseline for long-context latency. The paper also compares adjacent and global-anchor KV-sharing variants in ablations.
Regime: Dense models at 0.5B–1.5B and MoE models at 3B–16B total parameters; long-context inference reported for 9B MLA and 16B GQA at 8K–128K context with fixed 2K generation length.

Limitations: The performance and latency results are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this activation.; The long-context latency comparison is limited to 9B MLA and 16B GQA configurations, contexts of 8K–128K, and a fixed 2K generation length.; The reported 16B MMLU-Pro gain is a within-paper benchmark result; no independent evaluation, error bars or multi-seed reproduction was inspected.; The linked project code and detailed evaluation artifacts were not inspected or run; production deployment and serving economics are not established.

Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of reported quality, KV-cache or latency results was located or performed; linked code was not inspected.; The paper does not establish whether the reported benefits transfer to other architectures, production serving stacks or workload distributions.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03142

items: A Qwen looping study reports gains only in its smallest post-training regime — importance 5/10 · The authors compare post-training transformer layer loops in Qwen3/Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters against identically trained unlooped twins and unlooped equal-FLOP controls. In the reported short full-fine-tuning condition, the 0.8B loop improves a paired GSM8K/MATH macro score by 4.1 points, while the main 4B and 9B comparisons show no statistically significant gain. The paper separately evaluates training-free loop conversions: its Qwen3-8B loop has modest or non-significant task gains at about 1.8x measured decoding time, while selected Qwen3-14B results differ. These are author-reported results from specific Qwen recipes and task sets, not evidence about recurrence learned during large-scale pretraining or production workloads. — FCMO-649A811A9ED8

The Georgia PSC docket page checked on 3 November still lists docket 44280 as open, shows no filing rows, and provides no result or order for the Oct 29 hearing. Actual curtailment, avoided infrastructure and customer savings remain unmeasured. — FCMO-0FEC82980522

SafeWebWorld finds plausible web-agent predictions can still omit authorization evidence — importance 4/10 · A 29 Oct 2026 arXiv preprint introduces SafeWebWorld, a five-domain benchmark asking whether predicted web actions preserve evidence needed to choose among Execute, Ask, and Block. The authors report that 86.1% of 3,000 matched predictions from ten frozen open models were judged semantically plausible, while plausibility and low false-safe rates could coexist with weak evidence recovery or poor Ask recall. These are author-reported results on constructed cases: one primary reviewer audited the frozen test set, shortcut features remain predictive, and live action outcomes were not tested. — FCMO-6308BEA39DD1

items: KAPPO derives adaptive policy pressure for pass@k and max@k post-training — importance 5/10 · The authors derive closed-form optimal policies for KL-regularized pass@k and max@k objectives and identify prompt-adaptive pressure that can be implemented by modifying standard @1 optimization. They report experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation using OLMo-3-7B-Instruct-SFT and Qwen3-4B-Base: KAPPO variants reduce the paper's measured sharpening pattern, and @k-A*PO using one new completion per prompt is reported comparable to PKPO, which requires at least k on-policy completions. These are paper-reported results, not independent reproductions. — FCMO-8F63169BEDA5

blocks.text: training_data

items: Authors report that rare training facts raise LLM discovery rates in two controlled scientific domains — importance 5/10 · A 2 November 2026 preprint studies whether facts seen once in training are linked to language-model discovery capacity. In experiments on materials-science and regulatory-genomics tasks, the authors report that raising the share of these “monofacts” increases exact recovery of held-out target materials or DNA sequences across two open-weight model families. Repeated exposure weakens the trend while holding training-set diversity fixed. In-distribution, higher monofact rates also raise hallucinated outputs; cross-domain effects require in-domain training data.
